title: NVIDIA and Mediatek Ink $3.5B Investment Deal, Accelerate NVLink Fusion Adoption
gist: NVIDIA is investing $3.5B in MediaTek via convertible bonds while licensing MediaTek the full NVLink Fusion stack (Fusion chiplet, NVLink-C2C, NVHBM) so MediaTek's custom-silicon customers can build XPUs that plug into NVIDIA's rackscale ecosystem. The move is read as NVIDIA hedging against hyperscaler in-house accelerators by making itself the interconnect backbone rather than only a chip vendor, funded by a war chest built on nearly $60B of quarterly profit.

insights.claim: NVIDIA is investing $3.5 billion into MediaTek by purchasing convertible bonds issued by the Taiwanese fabless firm, rather than taking a straight equity stake.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A convertible structure gives NVIDIA optionality on MediaTek equity upside while keeping near-term dilution and regulatory optics low; watch for conversion terms as a marker of how much of MediaTek NVIDIA ultimately wants.
insights.quote: NVIDIA is investing $3.5B in MediaTek by purchasing convertible bonds issued by the company.
insights.locator: Under the terms of the deal

insights.claim: In exchange for the investment, MediaTek is adopting NVIDIA's complete NVLink Fusion technology stack — the Fusion chiplet, NVLink-C2C, and the new NVHBM memory protocol — to resell to its own custom-silicon customers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: MediaTek becomes a distribution channel for NVIDIA interconnect IP, expanding NVIDIA's attach rate into chips NVIDIA does not itself design.

insights.claim: The deal is explicitly aimed at MediaTek's custom chip business rather than MediaTek's in-house designs, making it materially more involved than the companies' prior GB10-era collaboration.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The economic exposure shifts from one SoC program to MediaTek's entire ASIC design-services pipeline, a much larger and more recurring revenue surface.
insights.quote: This latest deal is about custom chips rather than MediaTek’s in-house designs, so it is far more involved.
insights.locator: In some respects, it is surprising

insights.claim: Hyperscalers and large AI operators are increasingly building their own accelerators — Google's TPUs, Meta's MTIA, and OpenAI's Jalapeno are cited — signalling a structural hedge away from merchant GPUs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Custom-silicon programs are the main long-term threat to NVIDIA unit share; track their volume ramp as the key bear input for GPU TAM.
insights.quote: the hyperscalers are increasingly preparing to go their own way in the AI world, or at least, are hedging their bets

insights.claim: NVIDIA's counter-hedge is to give custom XPU developers easy access to the technologies needed to interface with NVIDIA's ecosystem, so that even non-NVIDIA accelerators are pulled inside NVIDIA's fabric.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: If custom silicon wins, NVIDIA still monetizes the rack, the fabric, and the chiplet — a partial floor under the bear case for GPU share loss.
insights.quote: So NVIDIA is hedging its bets as well, giving hyperscalers and other custom XPU developers more ready access to the technologies needed to interface with NVIDIA’s ecosystem.
insights.locator: As hyperscalers and other large AI operators

insights.claim: MediaTek's role pushes NVLink Fusion one level further down the stack: NVIDIA had been selling the technology directly to chip designers, and now a merchant ASIC house can offer it as part of its own design services.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Lowers the friction for tier-two AI chip programs to standardize on NVLink instead of Ethernet/UALink alternatives — a competitive negative for open-fabric consortia.
insights.quote: MediaTek’s announcement essentially pushes it one level down the stack by enabling it to offer it directly as well.
insights.locator: On the technology side of matters then

themes.theme: NVLink Fusion chiplet as the moat mechanism

insights.claim: The NVLink Fusion chiplet is a UCIe-attached fabric bridge that gives a third-party chip full NVLink fabric support while keeping NVLink's core internals a black box rather than licensed IP.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVIDIA gets ecosystem adoption without ever surrendering the protocol IP — the design that lets it open up without commoditizing itself.
insights.quote: while keeping the central components of NVLink as a black box to be integrated rather than licensing the IP itself
insights.locator: The most significant element of this technology offering

insights.claim: The Fusion chiplet is the critical enabler that lets custom XPUs plug into NVLink networks and NVIDIA's rackscale hardware ecosystem, tying third-party accelerators to NVIDIA rack economics.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Rack-level content, not just the GPU die, is where NVIDIA defends dollar share as accelerators diversify.
insights.locator: This is the critical part to enabling NVLink support

insights.claim: NVLink-C2C, the short-range chip-to-chip link principally used to bond custom CPUs to NVIDIA GPUs as in GB10, can also be used to link multiple XPUs or other chips together.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Widens the addressable use of NVIDIA interconnect beyond CPU-to-GPU attach into accelerator-to-accelerator topologies NVIDIA does not otherwise supply.
insights.locator: The MediaTek deal also includes NVLink-C2C support

insights.claim: NVHBM is a brand-new NVIDIA custom memory protocol that moves the memory controller onto the HBM base die instead of keeping it in the processor, and MediaTek will offer it to customers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shifting the memory controller into the HBM stack changes who captures value in the memory chain — watch HBM suppliers' base-die roadmaps and any NVIDIA-specific SKUs.
insights.quote: a custom memory protocol intended to connect processors to future generations of HBM, with the memory controller on the base die itself rather than part of the processor
insights.locator: Finally, MediaTek will also be offering

themes.theme: MediaTek's real role in NVIDIA silicon

insights.claim: Although the GB10 SoC inside NVIDIA's DGX and RTX Spark boxes is branded an NVIDIA chip, MediaTek did the majority of its development including the CPU cores and memory controller, with NVIDIA contributing the iGPU and chip-to-chip connectivity.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: MediaTek's design content in NVIDIA-branded products is far larger than the branding implies — a source of underappreciated revenue and strategic leverage.
insights.quote: MediaTek was responsible for the majority of the chip’s development, most notably its CPU cores and memory controller, while NVIDIA contributed the iGPU and the chip-to-chip connectivity that bonded the two.
insights.locator: Most notably, MediaTek was NVIDIA’s partner

insights.claim: The deal confirms NVIDIA will not bring future Spark chip development in-house, keeping MediaTek engaged across the Vera Rubin Spark and Rosa Feynman Spark generations on a roadmap running out to 2030.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Gives MediaTek multi-generation revenue visibility to the end of the decade and removes an in-sourcing risk that would otherwise hang over the relationship.
insights.quote: the deal confirms that NVIDIA will not bring the development of future Spark chips in-house

insights.claim: Beyond NVLink Fusion, the agreement extends the two companies' existing collaborations on Spark devices and automotive projects.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Automotive is a second, less-watched revenue vector in the partnership beyond the AI datacenter narrative.

themes.theme: NVIDIA's profits as a strategic war chest

insights.claim: NVIDIA reported nearly $60B in profits in its most recent quarter alone, giving it the balance sheet to fund equity-linked investments in partners and customers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: At that cash-generation rate a $3.5B investment is rounding-error capital, implying many more such deals are affordable and likely.
insights.quote: With nearly $60B in profits in their most recent quarter alone, NVIDIA has significant financial resources at its disposal.
insights.locator: At the same time, NVIDIA’s increasing use of its profits

insights.claim: The MediaTek deal is described as the latest in a series of NVIDIA investments in its partners and customers, indicating a deliberate program of using profits to bootstrap development at other tech firms.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Treat NVIDIA as an active strategic investor: announcements of stakes in suppliers, customers, and adjacent chipmakers are a recurring catalyst for those names.
insights.quote: a vision on how they want to use them to bootstrap developments at other tech firms
insights.locator: At the same time, NVIDIA’s increasing use of its profits

insights.claim: NVIDIA's ambition is characterized as becoming the backbone of the entire AI industry rather than remaining a hardware vendor or even an IP vendor.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes NVIDIA's valuation anchor from GPU unit share toward platform/fabric rents that persist even if accelerator share erodes.
insights.quote: NVIDIA is not content to be just a hardware vendor or even an IP vendor, and that it has greater ambitions to be the backbone of the entire AI industry

insights.claim: The deal brings no genuinely new technology to market — everything in it had already been unveiled by NVIDIA — so its significance is distributional and financial, not technical.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Avoid pricing this as a product catalyst; the tradeable content is channel expansion and NVIDIA's capital deployment posture.
insights.quote: Though the MediaTek deal does not bring any new significant technologies to the table that NVIDIA has not already unveiled
